clinical: Inflammation of the periosteum (periostitis) causes localised bone pain, because the fibrous layer is richly supplied with sensory nerves.
The cambium layer contributes the periosteal callus that bridges a fracture during healing.

Osteons.description: An osteon (Haversian system) is the basic structural unit of compact bone: concentric rings of bone matrix (lamellae) wrapped around a central (Haversian) canal that carries blood vessels and nerves. Osteocytes sit in small cavities called lacunae between the lamellae and connect with each other and with the canal through tiny channels called canaliculi. Osteons run roughly parallel to the long axis of the bone, so they appear as round cross-sections in a transverse section.
clinical: In Paget disease, osteoclasts resorb bone excessively and the replacement osteons form in a disorganised mosaic pattern, so affected bone is enlarged and weaker than normal.

Canals.description: Volkmann (perforating) canals run across the cortex, transversely or obliquely rather than along the long axis of the bone. They link central canals with each other and with the periosteal and marrow surfaces, and carry the vessels that join the periosteal and nutrient blood supplies. Unlike central canals, they have no concentric lamellae around them.

clinical: In osteoporosis, osteoclast resorption outpaces osteoblast bone formation during remodelling, thinning the trabeculae and cortex and raising fracture risk.
Bone marrow aspiration, usually from the posterior iliac crest or the sternum, samples red marrow to help diagnose blood disorders.

parts.description: Central (Haversian) canals are the narrow channels at the centre of each osteon, the cylindrical unit of compact bone, running along its long axis. Each canal is lined by endosteum, the thin membrane on internal bone surfaces, and carries the blood vessels and nerves that supply the osteon's bone. In cross-section they appear as small round holes surrounded by concentric rings of bone called lamellae, and Volkmann canals connect them to the periosteal and marrow surfaces.

Haversian arterioles and capillaries are the small arterial vessels and thin-walled capillaries that run through the central (Haversian) canal of each osteon. They supply oxygen to the bone, and nutrients reach the osteocytes from the canal through the canaliculi (tiny channels in the bone). In a section, an arteriole has a thicker, muscular wall than the venule beside it, which helps tell them apart.

Haversian venules are the thin-walled small veins that run in the central (Haversian) canal of each osteon, collecting blood from the capillaries. They carry deoxygenated blood and waste products out of the osteon towards the Volkmann canals and the larger veins of the bone. In a section, a venule is recognised by its thinner wall and wider lumen compared with the arteriole beside it.

Haversian nerve fibres are the thin nerve fibres that run inside the central (Haversian) canal of each osteon, alongside the blood vessels. They are mainly sensory fibres that carry pain signals, together with sympathetic fibres that help regulate blood flow in the bone. Nerve fibres are fine and hard to see on routine stains, so they are usually shown with silver or nerve-specific immunostains.

Concentric lamellae are the thin rings of mineralised bone matrix that wrap around the central (Haversian) canal of each osteon, like the layers of an onion. The collagen fibres in neighbouring lamellae run in alternating directions, which makes the osteon strong against twisting. In polarised light, the lamellae show alternating bright and dark bands because of this change in fibre direction.

Cement lines are thin layers of matrix, with few collagen fibres, that mark the boundary between each osteon and the older bone it has replaced. They form at reversal sites where osteoclast resorption has stopped and new bone formation has begun. In a section, a cement line appears as a thin, sharply outlined line curving around each osteon and bounding the interstitial lamellae.

Lamellar collagen fibres are the type I collagen fibrils that form the framework of each bone lamella, with hydroxyapatite mineral crystals deposited within and around them. The fibres in one lamella run roughly parallel to each other, and their direction changes from one lamella to the next. This layered arrangement gives compact bone its resistance to twisting and bending, and it is what makes the lamellae show bright and dark bands under polarised light.

Osteocytes are the mature bone cells that sit in small cavities called lacunae, scattered between the lamellae of both compact and spongy bone. Each osteocyte is star-shaped, and its long processes run through the canaliculi to contact neighbouring osteocytes. Osteocytes sense mechanical strain and help control bone remodelling, and in a section they appear as small, dark, oval nuclei sitting inside a lacuna.

Canaliculi are the very fine channels that radiate from each lacuna through the bone matrix, linking neighbouring lacunae with each other and with the central canal. Each carries a thin cell process of an osteocyte, and nutrients and signals pass between these processes through gap junctions. Because they are too narrow to resolve well in routine sections, they are seen most clearly in ground sections or with silver stains.

Volkmann canal vessels are the small arteries, capillaries and veins that run through the perforating (Volkmann) canals. They join the blood supply of the periosteum with that of the central canals and the marrow cavity, so that blood can pass between the outer and inner surfaces of the cortex. In a section, they appear as small vessel profiles inside a canal that has no concentric lamellae around it, and the arteries have a thicker muscular wall than the thin-walled veins beside them.

The Volkmann canal venule is a small, thin-walled vein that runs inside a perforating (Volkmann) canal across the cortex. It collects blood from the bone and carries it outwards to the periosteal veins or inwards to the marrow venous sinuses. In a section, it has a thinner wall and wider lumen than the arteriole in the same canal.

Inner circumferential lamellae are the thin, incomplete sheets of lamellar bone that line the marrow cavity just beneath the endosteum. They are laid down by endosteal osteoblasts on the marrow side of the cortex, and they are interrupted where trabeculae join the cortex. In a section, they appear as a thin, patchy band of parallel lamellae at the inner edge of the compact bone, facing the marrow.

Sharpey fibres are bundles of collagen from the periosteum that run obliquely into the outer circumferential lamellae, where they are partly calcified and anchor the periosteum to the bone. Tendons and ligaments attach to bone through these fibres at their entheses (attachment sites), and similar fibres fix the periodontal ligament in the tooth socket. In a section, they appear as pink, collagen-rich bundles running into the outer lamellae.

Periosteal arteries are the small branches of the periosteal plexus, the network within the periosteum that lies on the outer surface of bone. They supply roughly the outer third of the adult cortex by sending branches through Volkmann canals into the bone, while the nutrient artery supplies the inner two-thirds. Their role becomes vital when the medullary blood supply is damaged, for example by reaming of the marrow cavity before nail fixation.

Periosteal veins are the small veins of the periosteal plexus that drain the outer cortex and the periosteum itself. Blood from the outer cortex leaves through Volkmann canals and passes into these veins, which run alongside the periosteal arteries. Their walls are thinner than those of the neighbouring arteries, and in a section they are recognised by this thin wall and by lying alongside the muscular periosteal arteries.

Periosteal nerves are the nerve fibres that run within the periosteum, the membrane on the outer surface of bone. They include myelinated (A-delta) and unmyelinated (C) sensory fibres, which carry pain and temperature signals, as well as sympathetic fibres that control blood vessel tone. The periosteum is highly sensitive to pain, which is why fractures and periostitis (inflammation of the periosteum) are so painful.

Osteoblasts: plump cuboidal cells with basophilic (RNA-rich) cytoplasm, lined up on a surface where bone is forming over a thin seam of unmineralised osteoid. They secrete type I collagen, osteocalcin and alkaline phosphatase, control osteoclasts through RANKL (a signal that switches them on) and osteoprotegerin (a decoy that blocks RANKL), and end as osteocytes, flat lining cells or by apoptosis. Their development is controlled by the transcription factors RUNX2 and Osterix.

Bone-lining cells are flat, inactive cells that line bone surfaces where no bone is currently being formed or removed. They are derived from osteoblasts, and their thin, elongated, flattened nuclei distinguish them from the plump, active osteoblasts. When remodelling starts, they retract from the bone surface to expose it to osteoclasts, and they can be reactivated to become osteoblasts again.

Osteoclast nuclei are the several nuclei within each large, multinucleated osteoclast, a cell formed by fusion of monocyte-derived precursors. The nuclei share a single cytoplasm, so they appear as a cluster of small, dark, oval nuclei inside one large cell lying in a resorption pit. Counting the nuclei helps tell an osteoclast apart from osteoblasts and osteocytes, which have only one nucleus each.

Red (haematopoietic) marrow is the blood-forming tissue that fills the cavities of bone, consisting of thin-walled sinusoids set in a supporting mesh of reticular cells and fibres. It is packed with developing blood cells, including erythroblastic islands (clusters of developing red cells around a central macrophage), granulocyte precursors and megakaryocytes, the large cells that make platelets. In adults it is found mainly in the axial skeleton and the proximal ends of the femur and humerus, while the shafts of long bones contain yellow, fatty marrow.

Marrow adipocytes are the fat cells scattered among the blood-forming tissue of bone marrow. Each is unilocular, meaning it holds a single large fat droplet that pushes the nucleus and cytoplasm to one edge, giving a signet-ring appearance in sections. Their numbers rise with age and after radiotherapy or in aplastic anaemia, and the marrow of the long-bone shafts becomes yellow as they replace the blood-forming tissue.

A branch of the nutrient artery is an artery that enters the bone through the nutrient foramen (a small opening in the shaft) and then runs within the marrow cavity. It supplies the marrow and the inner two-thirds of the cortex, with endosteal branches passing into the Volkmann and central canals to reach the cortex. In a section, it is recognised by its thick muscular wall, which sets it apart from the thin-walled marrow sinusoids around it.

Marrow sinusoids are the wide, thin-walled vessels of the bone marrow, into which newly formed blood cells pass through gaps in the endothelium. They drain into the central venous sinus, a larger vein in the centre of the marrow cavity, which carries blood out of the bone through the nutrient vein. In a section, they are recognised by their wide, irregular lumens lined by a thin, flattened endothelium and set among developing blood cells.
